overview.zh: 背景:1999年,美国疾病控制与预防中心(CDC)建立了新疫苗监测网络(NVSN),作为多中心儿科传染病主动监测系统。方法:NVSN前瞻性地收集美国医院、急诊科、急救中心和门诊诊所中因急性呼吸道感染(ARI)或急性胃肠炎(AGE)症状就诊儿；目的:描述澳大利亚蜱引起的哺乳动物肉类过敏 (MMA) 的全国流行病学特征,包括 αGal 特异性 IgE 检测和病例检测的时间趋势、地理分布、人口统计风险因素和纵向抗体动态。设计:对 2014 年 1 月 1 日至 2024 年 12 月；口蹄疫病毒(FMDV)通过疫苗介导的选择压力驱动的适应性进化逃逸宿主免疫监视,导致免疫动物持续出现突破性感染。本研究分析了1980-2019年间分离的46株东南亚(SEA)和中东-南亚(ME-SA)拓扑型O型FMDV毒株中主要中和表位VP1

papers.title: The New Vaccine Surveillance Network: 25 years of active, population-based surveillance for pediatric infectious diseases in the United States.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: In 1999, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) established the New Vaccine Surveillance Network (NVSN) as a multi-site pediatric infectious diseases active surveillance system. METHODS: NVSN prospectively collects population-based clinical, epidemiologic, and laboratory information on children who seek medical care at hospitals, emergency departments, urgent care centers, and outpatient clinics with symptoms of acute respiratory infections (ARI) and acute gastroenteritis (AGE) in the United States. RESULTS: These efforts have clearly established the significant burden of both ARI and AGE in US children, demonstrated the effectiveness of licensed pediatric vaccines, and helped guide their use. The surveillance platform also measures the real-world impact of preventive measures intended to avoid or ameliorate adverse child health outcomes within the US healthcare system. Furthermore, NVSN provides a platform for detecting and evaluating emerging infections (e.g. enterovirus D-68, SARS-CoV-2) and unexpected sequelae in children. CONCLUSIONS: For 25 years NVSN has provided an evidence-based foundation for pediatric infectious disease policy decision-making through objective, empirical data. Sustained investment in disease surveillance guides the scientific principles and public health practices that prevent suffering and premature death, prepares us for new and existent pathogen threats, and enables wise economic decisions that improve the health of Americans.

papers.title: Tick-Induced Mammalian Meat Allergy in Australia: National Prevalence and Geographic Distribution from Laboratory Surveillance, 2014-2024
papers.abstract: Objectives: To characterise the national epidemiology of tick-induced mammalian meat allergy (MMA) in Australia, including temporal trends in αGal specific IgE testing and case detection, geographic distribution, demographic risk factors, and longitudinal antibody dynamics. Design: Retrospective analysis of αGal sIgE ImmunoCAPTM test results from 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2024. Setting, Participants: Deidentified laboratory records from 14,075 individuals tested across Australia, with residential postcodes mapped to Statistical Areas Level 3 (SA3). A subset of 1,515 individuals with repeat testing contributed to longitudinal analyses. Main outcome measures: Test volumes, suspected MMA case counts, positivity rates, spatial clustering metrics, demographic risk ratios, and longitudinal αGal sIgE trajectories. Results: Overall, 35.7% (5,025) of individuals tested positive. Testing volume increased 331% over the study period, with case detection accelerating sharply from 2020. Decomposition analysis attributed 59-81% of case growth to expanded testing, with the remainder unexplained by surveillance expansion alone. Cases were concentrated along the eastern seaboard within the range of Ixodes holocyclus, with extreme spatial clustering: three SA3 regions accounted for over one-quarter of national cases. Females comprised the majority of positive cases, and MMA risk increased with age, peaking at 45-74 years. Among 1,515 individuals with serial testing, αGal sIgE levels antibodies declined predictably in 93% of people. Conclusions: This first national assessment of MMA in Australia reveals a substantial, geographically concentrated, and growing burden. The extreme spatial concentration of cases suggests that targeted public health interventions could efficiently address a large proportion of national disease burden. While testing expansion is the dominant driver of rising case numbers, it does not fully account for observed trends, and prospective studies are needed to disentangle surveillance effects from genuine disease emergence. Declining antibody levels support the utility of serial testing for clinical monitoring, though persistent sensitisation underscores the need for sustained risk mitigation and continued surveillance.

Decomposition analysis attributed 59-81% of case growth to expanded testing, with the remainder unexplained by surveillance expansion alone. Cases were concentrated along the eastern seaboard within the range of Ixodes holocyclus, with extreme spatial clustering: three SA3 regions accounted for over one-quarter of national cases. Females comprised the majority of positive cases, and MMA risk increased with age, peaking at 45-74 years. Among 1,515 individuals with serial testing, αGal sIgE levels antibodies declined predictably in 93% of people. Conclusions: This first national assessment of MMA in Australia reveals a substantial, geographically concentrated, and growing burden. The extreme spatial concentration of cases suggests that targeted public health interventions could efficiently address a large proportion of national disease burden. While testing expansion is the dominant driver of rising case numbers, it does not fully account for observed trends, and prospective studies are needed to disentangle surveillance effects from genuine disease emergence. Introduction 69 Mammalian meat allergy (MMA), also known as alpha-Gal syndrome, is an 70 IgE‐mediated allergic condition characterised by delayed-onset hypersensitivity reactions to 71 galactose‐α‐1,3‐galactose (a‐Gal), an oligosaccharide abundant in non‐primate mammalian 72 tissues. Unlike typical food allergies, MMA is distinguished by a characteristic 3–8‐hour delay 73 between mammalian meat consumption and symptom onset, attributed to the time required for 74 digestion of a‐Gal–containing glycolipids [1]. The clinical spectrum of MMA ranges from mild 75 urticaria and gastrointestinal symptoms to life‐threatening anaphylaxis, with severe reactions 76 reported in up to 60% of affected individuals [2]. Beyond mammalian meat, reactions may 77 occur following exposure to mammalian‐derived products including dairy, gelatine, and 78 pharmaceuticals or medical devices bearing a‐Gal such as cetuximab and porcine heart valves 79 [3]. Australia's first confirmed MMA fatality was confirmed posthumously in February 2026, 80 following the first reported fatal case in the United States in 2025 [4, 5]. MMA presents 81 significant diagnostic challenges due to its delayed reaction, variable clinical manifestations, 82 and lack of clinician and public awareness of the condition [6, 7]. 83 MMA is induced by tick (Acari: Ixodidae) bites, with cases reported in at least 50 84 countries [8]. MMA has been attributed to various tick species worldwide, with the eastern 85 paralysis tick (Ixodes holocyclus) the established causative species in Australia [9, 10]. Ixodes 86 holocyclus is distributed along Australia’s eastern seaboard, co‐occurring with approximately 87 50% of Australia’s population, including major population centres in south-east Queensland 88 (QLD) and New South Wales (NSW) [11, 12]. Within its range, I. holocyclus accounts for 89 almost all reported human tick bites due to its generalist host preference and prevalence in peri- 90 urban residential settings and outdoor recreation areas [12, 13]. 91 Our understanding of MMA has advanced substantially in recent years, though 92 significant knowledge gaps remain, particularly in Australia, where comprehensive 93 epidemiological data are lacking. Previous estimates of MMA prevalence in Australia were 94 limited to a single region (approximately 113 cases per 100,000 in the Sydney Basin), derived 95 from clinical cohorts rather than systematic surveillance [8]. Consequently, the true burden of 96 MMA in Australia remains poorly characterised, hampering clinical recognition and leaving 97 clinicians, public health authorities, and policymakers without the evidence base needed to 98 respond to this emerging health threat. 99 This study addresses these gaps by analysing a-Gal-specific IgE (sIgE) testing data 100 from Australian pathology providers over an 11‐year period (2014–2024, inclusive). We sought 101 to characterise the burden and geographic distribution of MMA nationally, identify 102 demographic risk factors, examine temporal trends in testing and case detection, and describe 103 longitudinal changes in a-Gal sIgE levels among patients with repeated testing. These data 104 provide the first comprehensive epidemiological assessment of MMA in Australia and establish 105 baseline metrics for ongoing surveillance of this emerging allergic condition. 106 107 2. Methods 108 2.1 Data collection and processing 109 Deidentified data were obtained from all a-Gal sIgE ImmunoCAPTM (Phadia AB, 110 Uppsala, Sweden) tests submitted to QML Pathology, Sullivan & Nicolaides Pathology, 111 Douglass Hanly Moir Pathology, and Laverty Pathology between January 1, 2014, and 112 December 31, 2024. These laboratories provide services across all Australian states and 113 territories and conduct the majority of a-Gal sIgE testing in Australia. Although the exact 114 proportion of total national testing these providers represent is unknown, the authors were 115 unable to find other public or private pathology services that offered this test. Each record 116 contained a unique deidentified patient and test identifier, year of birth, sex, residential 117 postcode, date of test, and the test result in kilounits of a-Gal sIgE (kU/L). Clinical records, 118 travel histories, and any other tests results were not obtained. Data with invalid postcodes or 119 those from outside Australia or missing essential information were excluded (n=5). 120 Patients with at least one positive result (α-Gal sIgE ≥ 0.1 kU/L) were classified as 121 suspected MMA cases. In the absence of clinical data, this classification acknowledges that a 122 positive result provides supportive but not confirmatory evidence of MMA and assumes that 123 testing was requested based on clinical suspicion of MMA. However, we acknowledge that test 124 indications may have varied and could include investigation of idiopathic anaphylaxis or tick- 125 bite reactions. For patients receiving multiple positive tests demographic and location data were 126 taken from their first positive test. 127 Residential postcodes were aggregated to Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) 128 Statistical Areas Level 3 (SA3) regions (Australian Statistical Geography Standard Edition 3) 129 using spatial intersection analysis, assigning each postcode to the SA3 with the greatest 130 geographic overlap using the sf package in R v4.4 [14, 15]. SA3 regions represent functional 131 population areas of 30,000–130,000 people, providing a meaningful unit for regional 132 comparison. Suspected MMA cases were expressed as cases per million population per year 133 (PPY) for each SA3 region, using annual ABS regional population estimates as denominators. 134 135 2.2 Statistical analysis 136 Temporal trends in testing volume and case numbers were characterised using 137 segmented regression to identify breakpoints in growth trajectories. Demographic risk ratios 138 were calculated by age, sex, and age-sex combinations. Geographic analyses quantified spatial 139 heterogeneity in MMA burden using the Gini coefficient and spatial autocorrelation using 140 Moran's I. To quantify the extent to which increased case detections reflected expanded testing 141 versus genuine changes in sensitisation prevalence, we decomposed case growth into volume, 142 positivity rate, and interaction components using the pooled 2018–2020 period as the reference 143 baseline. This decomposition was extended to separate geographic expansion (new SA3 144 regions tested) from testing intensification within existing regions. Longitudinal antibody 145 dynamics were modelled using linear mixed-effects models to account for repeated measures 146 within patients. All analyses used R v4.4.1. Statistical tests are specified in Results with 147 corresponding p-values; two-sided p < 0.01 was considered significant unless otherwise noted. 148 The full analytic workflow, including all code used in this study, is available at 149 https://github.com/alexandergofton/Tick-Induced_MMA_in_Australia. 150 151 2.3 Ethics 152 This study was approved by the CSIRO Health and Medical Research Ethics 153 Committee (approval #2025_003_LR). As this study used retrospectively collected, 154 deidentified laboratory data with no patient contact, individual consent was not required. 155 156 3. Results 157 3.1 Patient population and demographic risk factors 158 From 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2024, 16,562 α-Gal sIgE ImmunoCAPTM tests 159 were performed on 14,075 people, with just 10.8% (1,515) of people receiving multiple tests 160 (range 2-15). Over the study period, 35.7% (5,025) of people tested were positive for α-Gal 161 sIgE (≥ 0.01kU/L) and were classified as suspected MMA cases. Females predominated among 162 those tested (64.8%) and positive cases (58.6%) (Table 1; Figure 1). Testing volume peaked 163 in the middle age (median age 48-49 years; Table 1; Figure 1A), with suspected MMA cases 164 being moderately older than those testing negative (Wilcoxon: p < 0.01; Kolmogorov-Smirnov: 165 p < 0.01; Cohen's d = 0.33), with peak positivity occurring at ages 55-74 for males and 45-74 166 for females (Table 1; Figure 1B). Despite lower testing rates, males had overall higher 167 positivity rates than females (42.0% vs 32.3%) (Tables 1, S1). 168 Age-and-sex stratified analysis using females aged 25–34 years as reference (18.5% 169 positivity; n = 1,220) revealed males aged 65–74 years as the group with the highest likelihood 170 of returning a positive test (53.9% positivity; RR = 2.91), followed by males aged 55–64 and 171 females aged 65–74 (Table S1; Figure S1). Within each age category, males consistently 172 demonstrated higher positivity rates than females. The 35.4 percentage point difference in 173 positivity between the lowest-positivity group (females 25–34) and the highest-positivity group 174 (males 65–74) suggests that both advancing age and male sex contribute to α-Gal sIgE 175 sensitisation risk among those tested (Table S1). However, despite males' higher positivity 176 rates, females comprised the majority of both tested individuals and positive cases (Table 1). 177 These patterns may reflect both underlying epidemiology and clinical testing behaviour which 178 could result in over‐representation of groups with higher perceived clinical suspicion. 179 180 3.2 Trends in Testing Volume and Case Detection 181 Testing volume 182 Alpha-Gal sIgE testing volume increased 331% from 628 tests in 2014 (609 people) to 2,707 183 tests in 2024 (2,155 people), with a significant acceleration in 2022 (Figure 2A; Table 1). 184 From 2014 to 2021, testing grew steadily at 136.7 tests/year (R2 = 0.79; CAGR: 12.5%, CI: 185 8.5-16.7). However in subsequent years (2022-2024), testing volume grew markedly, 186 increasing by 393 tests/year (R2 = 0.82; CAGR: 24.7%, CI: 9.8-41.6). Segmented regression 187 confirmed this 2022 breakpoint as a structural shift in testing practices (SE = 1.26, R2 = 0.93, 188 p < 0.01). This growth was driven by two simultaneous processes: geographic expansion (SA3 189 regions conducting testing increased from 152 to 254) and intensification within existing 190 regions (mean tests per region rose from 4.0 to 8.5 per year) (Figure 3A-C; Figure S2). 191 Regions that began testing later (≥2022) had significantly lower positivity rates than early- 192 adopter regions (≤2016; Kruskal–Wallis χ2 = 36.8, p < 0.01), suggesting initial testing was 193 concentrated in high-prevalence areas before expanding into lower-burden regions. Detailed 194 decomposition analysis is provided in Supplementary Information. 195 Suspected MMA case detections 196 Suspected MMA case detections increased 120.4% over the study period, from 357 in 197 2014 to 787 in 2024, with a breakpoint in 2020, two years before the testing volume breakpoint 198 (Table 1; Figure 2B). From 2014–2020, annual case numbers remained relatively stable, 199 increasing by just 6.68 cases/year (R2 = 0.91). From 2020 onwards, case detection accelerated 200 markedly at 110.2 cases/year (R2 = 0.84), representing a 121.1% increase. Testing positivity 201 rates also displayed two phases with a 2019 breakpoint (SE = 1.5, R2 = 0.76, p < 0.01; Figure 202 2C): an initial decline from 58.6% (2014) to 29.1% (2019) at −5.2%/year, likely reflecting 203 diagnostic selection bias when testing was largely restricted to patients with high clinical 204 suspicion, followed by an increase to 36.5% in 2024 at 1.2%/year, notably despite a 75.2% rise 205 in testing volume over the same period. 206 While testing expansion is the dominant driver of case growth, 19–41% of the observed 207 increase could not be attributed to surveillance expansion alone (Figure S3). To quantify this, 208 we decomposed case growth using the 2018–2020 period as the reference baseline, by which 209 time testing had stabilised into a representative referral pattern (mean positivity 30.3%). 210 Negative binomial regression confirmed that a time trend in positivity remained significant 211 after controlling for testing volume (rate ratio = 0.966 per year, CI 0.94–0.99; p < 0.05) 212 (Supplementary Information). 213 214 3.3 Geographic distribution of suspected MMA cases 215 Suspected MMA cases predominantly occurred along Australia’s east coast within the 216 range of the causative tick I. holocyclus (Figure 4). However, cases were recorded from every 217 state and territory, with 166 (3.8%) cases identified outside the tick’s recognised range, likely 218 reflecting exposure during travel or prior residence in endemic areas. 219 Within the I. holocyclus-endemic zone, suspected MMA cases showed striking 220 geographic clustering across SA3 regions, with a Gini coefficient of 0.86 (CI: 0.83–0.89). This 221 extreme spatial inequality, approaching the theoretical maximum of 1.0, indicated that the 222 majority of Australia’s MMA burden was concentrated in a small subset of SA3 regions 223 (Figure 5). Spatial autocorrelation analysis confirmed significant positive clustering (Moran’s 224 I: 0.291, p < 0.01), demonstrating that regions with high MMA burdens were geographically 225 proximate rather than randomly distributed. When adjusted for population size, just three SA3 226 regions accounted for 25.3% of the total MMA burden, 9 regions accounted for 52%, and 20 227 regions accounted for 70.7% (Figure 5). 228 To assess whether geographic clustering reflected selective referral to high-awareness 229 clinicians rather than true disease distribution, we analysed 6,404 tests with available referring 230 clinician postcodes. analysis.background: The study aims to characterise the national epidemiology of tick‑induced mammalian meat allergy (MMA) in Australia, addressing the previously unknown scale, temporal trends, geographic distribution and risk factors of this tick‑borne IgE‑mediated condition (A1).
analysis.methods: A retrospective analysis of α‑Gal specific IgE ImmunoCAP™ test results from 1 Jan 2014 to 31 Dec 2024 was performed (A2); de‑identified records from 14,075 tested individuals across Australia were linked to SA3 postcodes (A3); a subset of 1,515 individuals with repeat testing enabled longitudinal assessment (A4); outcomes included test volumes, case counts, positivity rates, spatial clustering, demographic risk ratios and antibody trajectories (A5).
analysis.results: Overall 35.7% (5,025) of tested persons were positive (A6); testing volume rose 331% with case detection accelerating sharply from 2020 (A7); 59–81% of case growth was attributable to expanded testing, leaving a residual increase unexplained (A8); cases clustered along the eastern seaboard within the Ixodes holocyclus range, with three SA3 regions accounting for >25% of national cases (A9); females predominated and risk peaked at ages 45–74 years (A10); among repeat testers, α‑Gal sIgE levels declined predictably in 93% of people (A11).
analysis.contribution: The paper provides the first national assessment of MMA in Australia, revealing a substantial, geographically concentrated and growing burden (A12); it highlights that targeted public‑health actions in a few high‑incidence regions could efficiently reduce national disease impact (A13); and it demonstrates that serial sIgE testing can monitor clinical status, supporting ongoing risk mitigation (A15).
analysis.limitations: The authors note that while testing expansion drives most of the observed increase, prospective studies are needed to separate surveillance artefacts from true disease emergence (A14); the retrospective laboratory‑based design limits inference about clinical outcomes or causality.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The study aims to characterise the national epidemiology of tick‑induced mammalian meat allergy (MMA) in Australia, addressing its previously unknown scale and risk factors (A1). Methods: Retrospective analysis of α‑Gal sIgE ImmunoCAP™ results from 2014‑2024 on 14,075 individuals linked to SA3 postcodes, with 1,515 repeat testers for longitudinal analysis (A2‑A5). Results: 35.7% (5,025) tested positive; testing rose 331% with case detection accelerating from 2020; 59–81% of case growth due to expanded testing; cases clustered on the east coast, three SA3s >25% of cases; females predominated, risk peaked at 45‑74 years; 93% showed predictable antibody decline (A6‑A11). Contribution: First national MMA assessment showing a substantial, geographically concentrated, growing burden; suggests targeted interventions could efficiently reduce disease impact and supports serial testing for monitoring (A12‑A15). Limitations: Prospective studies are needed to disentangle surveillance effects from true emergence; retrospective lab data limit causal inference (A14).

papers.abstract_zh: 目的:描述澳大利亚蜱引起的哺乳动物肉类过敏 (MMA) 的全国流行病学特征,包括 αGal 特异性 IgE 检测和病例检测的时间趋势、地理分布、人口统计风险因素和纵向抗体动态。设计:对 2014 年 1 月 1 日至 2024 年 12 月 31 日的 αGal sIgE 免疫CAPTM 测试结果进行回顾性分析。背景、参与者:来自澳大利亚各地 14,075 名测试者的去识别化实验室记录,住宅邮政编码映射到 3 级统计区域 (SA3)。对 1,515 名重复测试的个体进行了纵向分析。主要结果指标:测试量、疑似 MMA 病例数、阳性率、空间聚类指标、人口风险比和纵向 αGal sIgE 轨迹。结果:总体而言,35.7% (5,025) 的人检测呈阳性。在研究期间,检测量增加了 331%,病例检测从 2020 年开始急剧加速。分解分析将 59-81% 的病例增长归因于扩大检测,而其余部分则无法仅通过监测扩大来解释。病例集中在全环硬蜱分布范围内的东部沿海地区,具有极端的空间聚集性:三个SA3区域占全国病例的四分之一以上。女性占阳性病例的大多数,MMA 风险随着年龄的增长而增加,在 45-74 岁达到顶峰。在 1,515 名接受连续检测的人中,93% 的人的 αGal sIgE 抗体水平如预期下降。结论:澳大利亚 MMA 的首次全国评估揭示了巨大的、地域集中的、且不断增长的负担。病例的极端空间集中表明,有针对性的公共卫生干预措施可以有效解决很大一部分国家疾病负担。虽然检测范围的扩大是病例数量上升的主要驱动因素,但它并不能完全解释观察到的趋势,并且需要前瞻性研究来区分监测效果与真正的疾病出现。抗体水平下降支持了临床监测中连续检测的实用性,尽管持续的致敏强调了持续风险缓解和持续监测的必要性。

analysis_zh.background: 该研究旨在描述澳大利亚蜱引起的哺乳动物肉类过敏 (MMA) 的全国流行病学特征,解决这种蜱传播 IgE 介导的疾病的先前未知的规模、时间趋势、地理分布和风险因素 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 对2014年1月1日至2024年12月31日的α-Gal特异性IgEImmunoCAPTM检测结果进行回顾性分析(A2);来自澳大利亚各地 14,075 名测试者的去识别化记录与 SA3 邮政编码 (A3) 相关联;1,515 名重复测试的个体子集启用了纵向评估 (A4);结果包括测试量、病例数、阳性率、空间聚类、人口风险比和抗体轨迹 (A5)。
analysis_zh.results: 总体而言,35.7%(5,025)的检测者呈阳性(A6);检测量较 2020 年增长 331%,病例发现速度急剧加快 (A7);59-81% 的病例增长归因于扩大检测,导致剩余的增长无法解释 (A8);病例集中在全环硬蜱分布范围内的东部沿海地区,其中三个 SA3 地区占全国病例的 25% 以上 (A9);女性占主导地位,风险在 45-74 岁达到峰值 (A10);在重复测试者中,93% 的人的 α-Gal sIgE 水平按预期下降 (A11)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该文件提供了澳大利亚对 MMA 的首次全国评估,揭示了巨大的、地域集中的且不断增长的负担 (A12);它强调,在一些高发地区采取有针对性的公共卫生行动可以有效减少国家疾病的影响(A13);它表明连续 sIgE 检测可以监测临床状态,支持持续的风险缓解 (A15)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 作者指出,虽然测试扩展推动了大部分观察到的增长,但仍需要前瞻性研究将监测假象与真正的疾病出现区分开来 (A14);基于实验室的回顾性设计限制了对临床结果或因果关系的推断。

papers.title: Adaptive Evolution of Serotype O Foot‐and‐Mouth Disease Virus Under Vaccine Pressure: Combined VP1 T142/Q153 Mutations Drive Antigenic Alteration and Immune Evasion
papers.abstract: Foot‐and‐mouth disease virus (FMDV) escapes host immune surveillance via adaptive evolution driven by vaccine‐mediated selective pressure, leading to persistent breakthrough infections in immunized animals. In this study, the dominant neutralizing epitope VP1 G–H loop (141–160 aa) was analyzed among 46 serotype O FMDV strains belonging to Southeast Asian (SEA) and Middle East–South Asian (ME‐SA) topotypes isolated during 1980–2019. The key amino acid residues at VP1 positions 142 and 153 underwent sequential stepwise evolution across three phases under natural selection. Based on the reverse genetic system of Wt, single‐site mutant (T142P, Q153P) and double‐site mutant (T142P&Q153P) strains were rescued. These mutation sites were further introduced into an efficient FMDV nanoparticle vaccine to construct four vaccine candidates. Mouse immunization verified all vaccines conferred solid protection against Wt and single‐mutant strains, yet protection efficacy was greatly impaired against the double mutant. The double‐mutant vaccine elicited high‐level neutralizing antibodies against the double‐mutant strain (T142P&Q153P) with a titer of 1:426.67, 10–20 folds higher than Wt (1:21.33), T142P (1:32), and Q153P (1:42.67) vaccines. Consistent results were also obtained in pigs immunized with commercial inactivated vaccines. Collectively, combined mutations at VP1 142 and 153 reshape viral antigenicity and act as core drivers of FMDV immune evasion. Integrating such immune escape hotspots into vaccine antigens can broaden neutralizing antibody coverage, offering an experimental basis for clarifying FMDV evolution and developing broad‐spectrum vaccines.

analysis.summary_en: Background: FMDV evades immunity via vaccine‑driven adaptive evolution, causing breakthrough infections. papers.title: Discovery of non-nucleoside inhibitors of the enterovirus D68 3D polymerase through crystallographic fragment and high-throughput biochemical screening
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is a non-polio picornavirus that has caused increasing rates of severe respiratory illness and acute flaccid myelitis in children worldwide this century. There are no approved vaccines or antivirals for EV-D68. Thus, we conducted a crystallographic fragment screening (CFS) and a high-throughput screening (HTS) biochemical assay against the EV-D68 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase 3D (3D pol ) to identify ligandable sites and non-nucleoside compounds that can spearhead anti-enteroviral drug discovery. The CFS, involving 650 fragments, identified 68 hit compounds (~10% hit rate) distributed across 3D pol , including the functionally relevant sites RNA template channel, Active site, and RNA primer channel, and the previously unknown “Thumb site II” and “Index-middle finger pocket”. Inhibition assays confirmed that compounds binding to each site can inhibit EV-D68 3D pol activity. The HTS, a fluorescence-based PicoGreen biochemical assay, permitted screening 50,000 compounds of the ChemBridge Premium Library (0.77% hit rate). After a second-round dose-response screening, we identified 5-aminoindazole as a promising scaffold that inhibits EV-D68 3D pol , including hit-to-lead compound 727590, which displayed an IC 50 value of 25 μM and preliminary structure-activity relationships. These hits offer amenable starting points for discovery and development of non-nucleoside inhibitors and provide opportunities for structure-based drug design against enteroviruses. Thus, we conducted a crystallographic fragment screening (CFS) and a high-throughput screening (HTS) biochemical assay against the EV-D68 RNA-dependent RNA polymerase 3D (3Dpol) to identify ligandable sites and non-nucleoside compounds that can spearhead anti- enteroviral drug discovery. The HTS, a fluorescence-based PicoGreen biochemical assay, permitted screening 50,000 compounds of the ChemBridge Premium Library (0.77% hit rate). Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is an emerging viral pathogen belonging to the non-polio enterovirus group that has caused sporadic infections worldwide. It has primarily been detected in respiratory illnesses and is associated with occasional neurological infections (1). The pathogen can be detected in an infected person’s respiratory secretions, such as saliva and nasal mucus, hence, it can spread easily through cough and sneezes. EV-D68 was first isolated in California, USA, in 1962 and was recognized as a human pathogen responsible for various degrees of respiratory illness (2,3). Since then, many localized clusters of EV-D68 have been reported worldwide. In recent years, an outbreak occurred in Japan in 2010 with 88 cases (4). In 2012-2014, EV-D68 was detected in many children in polio-like infection clusters in California and Colorado (5). In 2014, EV-D68 caused unexpected widespread severe respiratory illness across North America with 1153 cases reported. This outbreak led to 3 deaths in Canada and 14 deaths in the USA (2). Since 2014, EV-D68 has emerged as a quasi-biennial epidemic in the United States and Europe, with the last significant outbreak in September 2022 (6). In some cases, EV-D68 has been found to cause polio-like paralysis called acute flaccid myelitis, which is associated with the sudden onset of weakness in the arms and legs due to brainstem and grey matter lesions (7,8). EV-D68 can cause serious complications, particularly in children and those with a weakened immune system (3). Due to this increased frequency of outbreaks and lack of vaccines and antiviral drugs, it is important to develop novel therapeutics against EV-D68. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) 3D, also known as 3Dpol, plays a key role in viral replication. Hence, it is highly conserved across different EV- D68 strains. 3Dpol initiates the synthesis of a negative-strand copy of the incoming viral genome to generate a double-stranded RNA replication intermediate. Then, the negative strand serves as a template for the synthesis of new positive-strand genome copies by 3Dpol, which are in turn used for translation or packed into new virions (9). RdRps catalyze RNA template-dependent formation of phosphodiester bonds between ribonucleotides in the presence of divalent metal ions (9,10). The initiation of 4 synthesis occurs at the 3′-end of the template using a small protein primer, named VPg, and proceeds in the 5′ to 3′ direction (11). To date, a significant number of crystal structures of RdRps from the picornavirus family have been reported. These include RdRps from poliovirus, coxsackieviruses A16 and B3, enteroviruses A71 and D68, human rhinoviruses 14 and 16, and foot-and-mouth disease virus, among others (12- 14). All RdRps (including the picornaviral) adopt a similar and conserved fold, resembling a cupped right hand with fingers, palm, and thumb subdomains. The fingers can be divided into different regions: pinky, ring, middle and index (Fig. S1). Besides exhibiting overall structural similarity, RdRps display seven conserved sequence motifs, namely A-G. Motifs A-D are shared between the single-subunit RNA and DNA polymerases, motifs E-F are unique to RdRps and reverse transcriptases (RTs), while motif G is an RdRp-specific structural element that interacts with the RNA template (13). Motifs A-E are located on the palm subdomain, which contains the active site in single- subunit polymerases and represents the most conserved region, while motifs F and G are part of the fingers’ subdomain (Fig. S1). Both motifs B and F participate in nucleotide triphosphate (NTP) substrate binding, interacting with the NTP ribose and triphosphate, respectively. Picornaviral RdRps also harbor motif H in their thumb subdomain, a specific motif found in single-stranded (+) RNA and dsRNA viruses, and participate in primer strand binding and protein stability (9,15). In addition to the three subdomains and eight structural motifs, EV-D68 3Dpol contains three channels arrayed with positive charge: the NTP entry channel, the RNA template channel, and the RNA exit channel (15). Crystallographic fragment screening (CFS) is a well-validated method for identifying novel compounds for the subsequent development of inhibitors (16-18). High-throughput screening (HTS) is a technique that enables rapid testing of millions of compounds for their biological activities via automated screening (19). Hit identification by CFS has the advantage of providing detailed information about the specific protein- ligand interactions and protein dynamics, as well as being very efficient at sampling the chemical space (20). Meanwhile, HTS offers the primary advantage of immense scale 5 and functional relevance, providing immediate evidence of enzymatic inhibition or biological activity under physiological-like conditions (21). With the aim of discovering novel non-nucleoside inhibitor scaffolds and leveraging the complementarity of both approaches, we have performed CFS and HTS campaigns targeting the EV-D68 3Dpol. The CFS has yielded 68 hits spanning three known sites—RNA template channel, Active site, RNA primer channel—and two previously unknown sites: the “Thumb site II”, and the “Index–middle finger pocket”. The HTS, using an enzymatic inhibition PicoGreen-based assay (19), has provided 388 initial hits, including a 5-aminoindazole scaffold with hit-to-lead compound 727590, displaying an IC50 value of 25 μM against EV-D68 3Dpol. The HTS enzymatic assay enabled the identification of single-site fragment hits across all five CFS binding sites. Functional validation demonstrated that fragments targeting each site inhibited enzymatic activity, confirming all newly identified sites are ligandable (except for the RNA template channel, previously validated) (15). Overall, our combined CFS and HTS campaigns provide valuable information for the design of follow-up compounds with higher binding affinity and activity inhibition of the EV-D68 3Dpol, as well as related RdRps from other viruses from the Picornaviridae family. MATERIALS AND METHODS Expression and purification The EV-D68 3Dpol gene was codon optimized for E. coli expression and synthesized by Genscript in the pET28a vector. The pET28a–EV-D68 3Dpol construct was transformed into E. coli BL21 (DE3) RIL cells and plated on LB agar with 50 μg/mL of kanamycin and 18 μg/mL chloramphenicol. A single colony was inoculated in 20 mL of Luria Broth (LB) media containing 50 μg/mL of kanamycin and 18 μg/mL chloramphenicol, followed by overnight incubation at 37 °C. This bacterial culture (A600 ~ 1) was added to one liter LB media containing 50 μg/mL of kanamycin and grown at 37 °C at 180 rpm of shaking until its optical density at 600 nm reached a value of 0.6. 6 Protein expression was induced with 0.5 mM Isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG, Bio) and incubated at 16 °C for 16 hours at 180 rpm. The cells were harvested at 4000g and resuspended in a lysis buffer containing, 50 mM HEPES (pH 8.0), 300 mM NaCl, 20% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM tris(2- carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP) and 1 mM phenylmethanesulfonylfluoride (PMSF). The cells were lysed by sonication and then centrifuged for 45 minutes at 44,000g (4 °C). The supernatant was passed through nickel-nitrilotriacetic acid (Ni-NTA) beads, followed by washing the unbound protein with the same buffer supplemented with lysis buffer supplemented with 10 mM and 20 mM imidazole respectively. The protein was eluted in a buffer containing 50 mM HEPES (pH 8.0), 300 mM NaCl, 20% (v/v) glycerol, and 200 mM imidazole, diluted to reduce the NaCl concentration to approximately 100 mM prior to loading onto a HiTrap Q HP column (GE Healthcare), equilibrated with buffer containing 50 mM Tris pH 8, 100 mM NaCl, 20% glycerol, and 1 mM TCEP. 3Dpol was eluted using a linear salt gradient from 100 mM NaCl to 500 mM NaCl. The peak fractions were pooled, concentrated and loaded onto a Superdex 200 column (GE Healthcare) equilibrated with buffer containing 50 mM HEPES (pH 7.6), 300 mM NaCl, 3% Glycerol, 50 mM MgCl2, and 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT). The eluted protein was concentrated to 12 mg/ml, aliquoted, flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80 °C for crystallization. Crystallization, structure determination, and optimization for fragment screening Crystals were grown in a crystallization solution comprising 0.1 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.5), 16% polyethylene glycol (PEG) 3350, and 16% isopropanol by sitting-drop vapor diffusion in MRC 3 Lens Crystallization plates (SWISSCI) at 16 °C, with 0.4 nl of the aforementioned reservoir solution, and a 1:1 v/v ratio of protein to crystallization solution. Initial data collection was carried out at the SSRL BL12-2 beamline, and the structure was solved by molecular replacement using the structure of EV-D68 3Dpol complexed to GTP (PDB code: 5XE0, with GTP and other heteroatoms removed) as a reference model using the Phaser program in the Phenix suite (22). The solvent tolerance of the crystals was checked by incubating the crystals with 10-30% dimethyl 7 sulfoxide (DMSO) for 1-3 hours at 20 °C and collecting the corresponding datasets also at the SSRL BL12-2 beamline. Fragment screening Around 650 crystals were grown in house and carried to the XChem facility at the Diamond Light Source, UK. Due to limitation in the number of crystals, we screened 650 fragments exclusively from the DSi-Poised Library (23). Fragments were soaked into drops containing EV-D68 3Dpol crystals at 20 % (v/v) DMSO using acoustic dispensing with an Echo 650 liquid handler (Labcyte) (24). After incubation for 2 hours at 20 °C, the crystals were harvested using the Crystal Shifter (Oxford Lab Technologies) (25), mounted on loops and cryo-cooled in liquid nitrogen without additional cryoprotectant. Data was collected at the I04-1 beamline (Diamond Light Source, UK) at 100 K and automatically processed with Diamond Light Source’s autoprocessing pipelines using XDS (26) and either xia2 (27), autoPROC (28), or DIALS (29) with the default settings. Analysis of fragment binding was done using XChemExplorer (30). Electron density maps were generated with DIMPLE (31), ligand restraints were calculated with ACEDRG (32) and GRADE (33), and ligand-binding events were identified using PanDDA2 (34,35). Ligands were modelled into PanDDA2-calculated event maps manually using Coot (36), and structures were refined with Refmac (37). Coordinates and structure factors for the ground-state (PDB 14AA) and ligand- bound EV-D68 3Dpol structures (group deposition G_1002366) discussed here are deposited in the Protein Data Bank. Data collection and refinement statistics are summarized in Supplementary Data File 1. High-throughput screening assay Primary screening using the fluorescence-based PicoGreen biochemical assay EV-D68 3Dpol RdRp activity was determined using a fluorescence-based biochemical assay, as previously described with minor modifications (19). EV-D68 3Dpol, expressed and purified as described above, was diluted to a final concentration of 5 μM 8 in assay buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 1 mM MgCl2, 0.005% Triton X-100, and PicoGreen (ThermoFisher, final concentration: 10 μl/ml). The enzyme solution was dispensed into 384-well low-volume black round-bottom microplate (Corning, Catalog No.: 4514) at2.5 μl per well using a Dragonfly liquid handler (SPT Labtech). Columns 23 and 24 were added assay buffer containing PicoGreen and remaining reagents, but not EV-D68 3Dpol, to serve as a positive value for 100% inhibition. Next, 10 nl of each compound from the ChemBridge Premium Library (50,000 compounds) was transferred into assay plates using an Echo 650 acoustic liquid handler (Beckman Coulter Life Science), and the resulting assay plates were centrifuged at 300g for 1 minute, followed by a 15-minute incubation in the dark. The assay buffer containing 5 μM template (sequence: 5’-UGCGCUAGUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUGAUCGCGU) and 200 μM dNTP mix (ThermoFisher) was then added to the plate, with a volume of 2.5 μl per well, using a Dragonfly liquid handler (SPT Labtech). Assay plates were then sealed, centrifuged at 300g for 1 minute, and incubated in the dark for 19 hours. Fluorescence was measured using an Envision multimode plate reader (PerkinElmer) with excitation and emission wavelengths at 485 nm and 520 nm, respectively. IC50 determination and counterscreen using the PicoGreen biochemical assay 35 compounds identified from the primary screening were selected for IC50 determination and counterscreen using the same assay described in the primary screening. All compounds were evaluated in duplicates using a 10-point dose-response curve. Unlike the primary screening, in the counterscreen, an assay buffer containing PicoGreen but lacking EV-D68 3Dpol was treated with compounds and then incubated with the assay buffer containing 5 μM RNA duplex (sequences: 5'- ACGCGAUCAAAAAAAAAA-3' and 5'-UUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUGA-3') and 200 μM dNTP mix. PicoGreen binding to the RNA duplex generates a high fluorescence signal. Compounds that reduced fluorescence in the absence of 3Dpol were classified as false positives. IC50 determination using a gel-based primer extension assay To validate the inhibition results of Z56040660, compound 727590 (HTS hit), and fragments RLA-6625 to RLA-6629, gel-based in vitro primer extension assays were performed similarly as previously described (38). The template and primer utilized were 9 3'-UGCGGUACUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUU-5' and 5'-pACGC-3', respectively. Reactions requiring non-5′-labeled primer were supplemented with 0.1 μM [α-32P]-CTP for visualization. Standard reaction mixtures (15 μl) consisted of purified EV-D68 3Dpol, assay buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, 2.5 mM MgCl2, 0.005% Triton X-100, pH 8.0), 200 μM primer, 2 μM template, and NTPs. The compounds (or the DMSO control) were pre- incubated for 20 min with enzyme only, and reactions were started by the addition of template, primer and NTPs and lasted 45 min at 30 °C. Reactions were stopped with equal volumes of a formamide, 50 mM EDTA mixture. Mixtures were boiled at 95°C for 5 min, and 3 μl samples resolved by 8 M urea, 20% polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. Radiolabeled or fluorescent signals were visualized using an Amersham Typhoon biomolecular imager and quantified in Cytiva ImageQuant TL software. Chemistry Chemical reagents were purchased from commercial suppliers as indicated above and used without further purification. See the Supplementary Data section for detailed methods of the synthesized fragments. Figure preparation High-resolution structural figures were prepared for publication using PyMOL (The PyMOL Molecular Graphics System, Version 2.5, Schrödinger, LLC) and BioRender (biorender.com). Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is an emerging viral pathogen belonging to the non-polio enterovirus group that has caused sporadic infections worldwide. It has primarily been detected in respiratory illnesses and is associated with occasional neurological infections (1). The pathogen can be detected in an infected person’s respiratory secretions, such as saliva and nasal mucus, hence, it can spread easily through cough and sneezes. EV-D68 was first isolated in California, USA, in 1962 and was recognized as a human pathogen responsible for various degrees of respiratory illness (2,3). Since then, many localized clusters of EV-D68 have been reported worldwide. In recent years, an outbreak occurred in Japan in 2010 with 88 cases (4). In 2012-2014, EV-D68 was detected in many children in polio-like infection clusters in California and Colorado (5). In 2014, EV-D68 caused unexpected widespread severe respiratory illness across North America with 1153 cases reported. This outbreak led to 3 deaths in Canada and 14 deaths in the USA (2). Since 2014, EV-D68 has emerged as a quasi-biennial epidemic in the United States and Europe, with the last significant outbreak in September 2022 (6). In some cases, EV-D68 has been found to cause polio-like paralysis called acute flaccid myelitis, which is associated with the sudden onset of weakness in the arms and legs due to brainstem and grey matter lesions (7,8). EV-D68 can cause serious complications, particularly in children and those with a weakened immune system (3). Due to this increased frequency of outbreaks and lack of vaccines and antiviral drugs, it is important to develop novel therapeutics against EV-D68. The viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) 3D, also known as 3Dpol, plays a key role in viral replication. Hence, it is highly conserved across different EV- D68 strains. 3Dpol initiates the synthesis of a negative-strand copy of the incoming viral genome to generate a double-stranded RNA replication intermediate. Then, the negative strand serves as a template for the synthesis of new positive-strand genome copies by 3Dpol, which are in turn used for translation or packed into new virions (9). RdRps catalyze RNA template-dependent formation of phosphodiester bonds between ribonucleotides in the presence of divalent metal ions (9,10). The initiation of 4 synthesis occurs at the 3′-end of the template using a small protein primer, named VPg, and proceeds in the 5′ to 3′ direction (11). To date, a significant number of crystal structures of RdRps from the picornavirus family have been reported. These include RdRps from poliovirus, coxsackieviruses A16 and B3, enteroviruses A71 and D68, human rhinoviruses 14 and 16, and foot-and-mouth disease virus, among others (12- 14). All RdRps (including the picornaviral) adopt a similar and conserved fold, resembling a cupped right hand with fingers, palm, and thumb subdomains. The fingers can be divided into different regions: pinky, ring, middle and index (Fig. S1). Besides exhibiting overall structural similarity, RdRps display seven conserved sequence motifs, namely A-G. Motifs A-D are shared between the single-subunit RNA and DNA polymerases, motifs E-F are unique to RdRps and reverse transcriptases (RTs), while motif G is an RdRp-specific structural element that interacts with the RNA template (13). Motifs A-E are located on the palm subdomain, which contains the active site in single- subunit polymerases and represents the most conserved region, while motifs F and G are part of the fingers’ subdomain (Fig. S1). Both motifs B and F participate in nucleotide triphosphate (NTP) substrate binding, interacting with the NTP ribose and triphosphate, respectively. Picornaviral RdRps also harbor motif H in their thumb subdomain, a specific motif found in single-stranded (+) RNA and dsRNA viruses, and participate in primer strand binding and protein stability (9,15). In addition to the three subdomains and eight structural motifs, EV-D68 3Dpol contains three channels arrayed with positive charge: the NTP entry channel, the RNA template channel, and the RNA exit channel (15). Crystallographic fragment screening (CFS) is a well-validated method for identifying novel compounds for the subsequent development of inhibitors (16-18). High-throughput screening (HTS) is a technique that enables rapid testing of millions of compounds for their biological activities via automated screening (19). Hit identification by CFS has the advantage of providing detailed information about the specific protein- ligand interactions and protein dynamics, as well as being very efficient at sampling the chemical space (20). papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 肠道病毒 D68 (EV-D68) 是一种非脊髓灰质炎小核糖核酸病毒,本世纪导致全世界儿童严重呼吸道疾病和急性弛缓性脊髓炎的发病率不断上升。目前还没有批准用于 EV-D68 的疫苗或抗病毒药物。因此,我们针对 EV-D68 RNA 依赖性 RNA 聚合酶 3D (3D pol ) 进行了晶体片段筛选 (CFS) 和高通量筛选 (HTS) 生化测定,以鉴定可引领抗肠道病毒药物发现的配位位点和非核苷化合物。CFS 涉及 650 个片段,鉴定了分布在 3D pol 上的 68 个命中化合物(命中率约 10%),包括功能相关位点 RNA 模板通道、活性位点和 RNA 引物通道,以及以前未知的“拇指位点 II”和“食指中指口袋”。抑制测定证实,与每个位点结合的化合物可以抑制 EV-D68 3D pol 活性。HTS 是一种基于荧光的 PicoGreen 生化检测,可筛选 ChemBridge Premium 库中的 50,000 种化合物(命中率 0.77%)。经过第二轮剂量反应筛选,我们确定 5-氨基吲唑是一种有前途的抑制 EV-D68 3D pol 的支架,其中包括命中先导化合物 727590,其 IC 50 值为 25 μM,并具有初步的构效关系。这些成果为非核苷抑制剂的发现和开发提供了良好的起点,并为基于结构的肠道病毒药物设计提供了机会。图形摘要 使用 biorender.com 和 PyMOL 分子图形系统 2.5.0 版创建。薛定谔有限责任公司。

papers.title: Meningococcal meningitis in India: An expert consensus on use of MCVs.
papers.abstract: Invasive meningococcal disease (IMD) is a significant but under-recognized public health challenge in India, marked by rapid progression, high mortality, and severe sequelae. This consensus document, developed from literature review, outbreak analyses, and deliberations by 14 Indian experts, highlights outbreaks from 1966 (Delhi: 616 cases, case fatality ration: CFR 20.9%) to 2022-2023 (Kolkata). Serogroup A remains predominant, with emerging serogroups C, W, and Y. Systematic review evidence shows 12.1% prevalence in epidemics (CFR 12.8%) and 0.76% in endemic settings (CFR 3.0%), though true burden is underestimated due to weak surveillance. IMD shows bimodal age distribution, highest in children < 5 y (61.8%) and adolescents. MenACWY conjugate vaccines show 95.7-99.5% seroprotection across serogroups. Experts recommend vaccination at 9-12 months with booster at 10-11 y, mandatory reporting, sentinel surveillance, and clinician awareness. The roadmap stresses awareness, short-term surveillance, and long-term data generation toward National Immunization Program inclusion.

papers.full_text: Meningococcal meningitis in India: An expert consensus on use of MCVs ABSTRACT Invasive meningococcal disease (IMD) is a significant but under-recognized public health challenge in India, marked by rapid progression, high mortality, and severe sequelae. This consensus document, developed from literature review, outbreak analyses, and deliberations by 14 Indian experts, highlights outbreaks from 1966 (Delhi: 616 cases, case fatality ration: CFR 20.9%) to 2022–2023 (Kolkata). Serogroup A remains predominant, with emerging serogroups C, W, and Y. Systematic review evidence shows 12.1% prevalence in epidemics (CFR 12.8%) and 0.76% in endemic settings (CFR 3.0%), though true burden is underestimated due to weak surveillance. IMD shows bimodal age distribution, highest in children < 5 y (61.8%) and adolescents. MenACWY conjugate vaccines show 95.7–99.5% seroprotection across serogroups. Experts recommend vaccination at 9–12 months with booster at 10–11 y, mandatory reporting, sentinel surveillance, and clinician awareness. The roadmap stresses awareness, short-term surveillance, and long-term data generation toward National Immunization Program inclusion. Background and context Neisseria meningitidis, a gram-negative diplococcus, causes life-threatening invasive meningococcal disease (IMD). IMD is characterized by rapid progression, high mortality (4–20%), and devastating long-term complications affecting 10–20% of survivors. Despite being a notifiable disease in India, meningococcal infection remains poorly documented due to diagnostic challenges, limited surveillance infrastructure, and low clinical suspicion outside outbreak settings. This expert consensus emerged from a comprehensive review of pre-published literature, outbreak reports from Indian settings, and deliberations among 14 expert pediatricians, infectious disease specialists, and microbiologists representing diverse geographic regions across India. Epidemiology and disease burden Serogroup A remains the predominant strain associated with outbreaks in India and accounts for most epidemic disease. Sporadic cases involving other serogroups have been increasingly documented. Serogroup C has been reported in pediatric cases from the Institute of Child Health, Kolkata during 2022–2023. Serogroup W-135 has been described in case reports from Tamil Nadu and other regions. Serogroup B has been noted in isolated reports from tertiary centers and, although uncommon, is reported in India. Serogroup X is not clinically significant in India and is relevant mainly to the African meningitis belt. The emergence of non-A serogroups in sporadic cases indicates changing epidemiological patterns and highlights the need for broader vaccine coverage beyond traditional outbreak-associated strains. Evolution of meningococcal serogroups globally. Serogroup Global Evolution Pattern A Dominated African meningitis belt until MenAfriVac introduction (2010); near-elimination by 2015 Also responsible for recurrent large outbreaks in India (Delhi epidemics in 1966–1967, 1985–1986, and 2005–2006 with high case fatality, Meghalaya in 2008–2009, Tripura in 2009). C Caused 20% of global IMD through mid-2010s; reduced by MCC/ACWY vaccine programs. In India, only sporadic serogroup C cases have been reported. (Note: MCC – Meningococcal C conjugate vaccine) W Emerged after 2000 Hajj outbreaks; increased endemic disease in South America, UK, Australia. Serogroup W has been documented infrequently in non‐outbreak settings and case reports, contributing a minor fraction of total reported IMD from India. Y Emerged in 1990s USA; accounts for 20–30% of US IMD cases; driving 2023–2024 US surge. Indian literature notes occasional serogroup Y cases and detectable carriage/antibody responses, but no confirmed serogroup Y outbreak and very low documented clinical burden. B Predominant in Europe, Americas, Australia; accounts for 50–70% of cases in high-income countries. This serotype is considered uncommon in India. X Historically caused sporadic and small outbreaks in the African meningitis belt; major localized epidemics reported in Niger, Burkina Faso, Togo and Kenya since mid‐2000s, with serogroup X responsible for up to ~50–56% of confirmed cases in some district‐level outbreaks. No documented outbreaks or established circulation in India to date. Globally, meningococcal disease showed a significant decline during the COVID-19 pandemic due to non-pharmaceutical interventions such as masking, physical distancing, and reduced travel. A rebound has been observed in the post-pandemic period with several concerning trends. Circulating strains with increased virulence have reemerged. New clonal complexes have appeared following the resumption of international travel. Population immunity has decreased in unvaccinated cohorts. The United States reported the highest number of cases since 2014, with 503 confirmed cases in 2024. There has also been a disproportionate impact on adults aged 30–60 y, Black or African American populations, and individuals with HIV. The summary of evolution of meningococcal serogroups is shown in Table 1. Historically, the evolution of meningococcal serogroups has shown dynamic global shifts. Serogroup A dominated the African meningitis belt until the introduction of MenAfriVac (Serogroup A conjugate vaccine) in 2010, leading to near-elimination by 2015. Serogroup C contributed to about 20% of global IMD through the mid-2010s but declined following MCC and ACWY vaccination programs. Serogroup W emerged after the 2000 Hajj outbreaks and later increased in endemic regions such as South America, the United Kingdom, and Australia. Serogroup Y, which emerged in the United States in the 1990s, now accounts for 20–30% of U.S. cases and is a major driver of the 2023–2024 surge. Serogroup B remains predominant in Europe, the Americas, and Australia and contributes to 50%–70% of cases in high-income countries. In the Asia-Pacific region, meningococcal disease remains under-recognized, largely due to inadequate surveillance systems. Serogroup A has historically been predominant in China, India, Nepal, Mongolia, and Pakistan. Emerging serogroups, including C, Y, and W, have been reported in several countries. Serogroup B is uncommon in most of Asia except in developed nations such as Australia, New Zealand, and Japan. The overall disease burden in the region is likely significantly underestimated. Meningococcal outbreaks in India. Place of Outbreak Year Cases Reported Deaths Reported Case Fatality Ratio (CFR) Reference Literature Delhi 1966 616 Not specified Not specified NCDC CD Alert 2009; PIB 2006 Delhi and adjoining areas 1985–1986 6133 799 13% NCDC CD Alert 2009; PIB 2006 Surat, Gujarat 1985–1987 197 34 17.3% NCDC CD Alert 2009; Bhavsar et al. 1989 Vishakhapatnam, Vijayanagram, Srikakulam (Andhra Pradesh) 1989 475 108 22.7% NCDC CD Alert 2009 Orissa 1989 2951 344 11.7% NCDC CD Alert 2009 Madhya Pradesh 1989 250 >75 >30% NCDC CD Alert 2009 Delhi and adjoining areas 2005–2006 444 62 13.90% Nair et al.; NCDC CD Alert 2009 Meghalaya 2008–2009 2100 260 12.4% NCDC CD Alert 2009 Tripura 2009 277 60 21.7% NCDC CD Alert 2009 India continues to experience both epidemic and endemic meningococcal disease. Indian data mostly come from outbreaks and hospital-based reports, as any systematic national surveillance is lacking. Major Indian outbreaks have been tabulated in Table 2. Meningococcal disease prevalence and mortality in India. Setting Prevalence Case Fatality Rate Epidemic conditions 12.1% (among suspected ABM) 12.8% Endemic conditions 0.76% 3.0% A systematic review and meta-analysis by Ghia et al. further quantified disease burden in India. Under epidemic conditions, the prevalence among suspected acute bacterial meningitis cases was 12.1% with a CFR of 12.8%. Under endemic conditions, prevalence was 0.76% with a CFR of 3.0%. It also reported that National Health Profile data from 2005 to 2012 demonstrated a 39% increase in reported cases, rising from 3397 in 2005 to 5609 in 2012, and a 25% increase in deaths from 311 in 2006 to 413 in 2012, indicating a rising disease burden in India. Meningococcal disease prevelence and mortality rate in India is summarized in Table 3. Geographically, disease incidence is higher in northern and northeastern states, forming a belt spanning Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Assam. Sporadic cases are increasingly reported from southern and western regions. Sentinel hospitals in Chennai and Pondicherry have detected sporadic cases. Isolated cases have been reported in Maharashtra, including Surat and Navi Mumbai. Gujarat recorded a historic outbreak between 1985 and 1987 with 197 cases. Emerging surveillance data are also available from Bangalore in Karnataka. The apparent north-south gradient may reflect surveillance disparities rather than true absence of disease in southern states, which is an important consideration when assessing national burden. Age-specific data from 110 cases in the Meghalaya outbreak (2008–2009) showed a bimodal distribution. The first peak occurred among children under five years of age, comprising 61.8% of cases. The highest risk was observed among infants aged 3–11 months, who also showed more rapid disease progression and severe outcomes. Nonspecific presentations in this age group often delayed diagnosis. The second peak occurred in adolescents and young adults aged 10–18 y, a group associated with crowding in schools, hostels, and dormitories, and higher nasopharyngeal carriage. Mass gatherings further increased the risk of transmission. Additional high-risk groups include immunocompromised individuals such as those with HIV, complement deficiencies, or asplenia; healthcare and laboratory personnel during outbreaks; military personnel; Hajj pilgrims and international travelers; and patients receiving biological therapies including rituximab, eculizumab, alemtuzumab, and tofacitinib. Routine, high-quality surveillance for meningococcal disease is still not established in India, so reliable information on the endemic burden remains limited because of weak surveillance networks and constrained laboratory capacity. Although the Integrated Disease Surveillance Program (IDSP) collects meningitis and meningococcal data, these datasets are not generally accessible in the public domain, meaning that the true patterns and incidence captured by IDSP cannot be independently assessed. Need for consensus: perspective from Indian subcontinent Challenges discussed in the meeting The expert panel deliberated extensively on multifaceted challenges hindering effective meningococcal disease prevention and management in India: Surveillance and data gaps Underreporting to IDSP and NCDC (National Centre for Disease Control) remains a major challenge. Although meningococcal disease is notifiable, reporting compliance is extremely poor. Cases from the private sector are rarely reported to public health authorities. Many clinicians are not fully aware of the reporting requirements, which further contributes to underreporting, underscoring the importance of proper training and CME sessions conducted by field experts and key opinion leaders (KOLs). Laboratory diagnostic capacity is also limited in different parts of India. Meningococcal-specific culture techniques are not widely available. PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) and other molecular diagnostic tools remain inaccessible in many settings. Serogroup typing is performed only at reference laboratories. Culture positivity is often low, especially when samples are collected after antibiotic administration, with yields of only 10–20%. Available data are fragmented. Most information comes from hospital-based studies conducted at selected tertiary centers, usually for short durations and with small sample sizes. There are no population-based estimates of incidence. Regional bias is evident, with more data coming from northern and northeastern regions than from southern and western parts of the country. Nasopharyngeal carriage data are extremely limited in India. There are very few studies assessing carriage, and no systematic evaluation of asymptomatic colonization rates. As a result, the carriage-to-disease ratio remains unknown. Clinical recognition limitations Expert consensus identified several diagnostic barriers. Early symptoms are nonspecific and often indistinguishable from common viral illnesses, particularly in infants. Many patients do not show the classic petechial or purpuric rash at initial evaluation, and only 25–30% present with this pathognomonic feature. The disease progresses rapidly, leaving a narrow window between the onset of symptoms and critical deterioration. Clinical features also overlap with other causes of bacterial meningitis, such as pneumococcal or Haemophilus meningitis, making differentiation difficult. Clinical suspicion remains low in many settings because numerous practitioners have never encountered a case outside of outbreak situations. Diagnostic challenges Current limitations in India include extremely low culture positivity (105–20% of suspected cases), fastidious growth requirements (CO2-enriched environment, chocolate agar), organism viability rapidly decreases post-antibiotic exposure, limited laboratory capacity for meningococcal-specific testing, and underutilization of available diagnostic modalities including filmarray. Vaccination policy and awareness gaps Introduction of meningococcal conjugate vaccines in national immunization programs has led to dramatic reductions (>90%) in targeted serogroups in European countries. In contrast, current Indian Academy of Pediatrics (IAP) guidelines classify the meningococcal vaccine as a recommendation only for high-risk groups., the vaccine is not included in the National Immunization Program (NIP), largely due to limited robust surveillance data, competing vaccine priorities such as HPV, pneumococcal, and rotavirus vaccines. Awareness among healthcare providers regarding the availability and effectiveness of meningococcal vaccines remains low. In addition, many families and even some clinicians hold the misconception that meningococcal disease occurs only in northern India or primarily during outbreaks. Meningococcal disease spectrum and severity discussed in the meeting Meningococcal disease presents with a wide clinical spectrum that ranges from asymptomatic carriage and mild bacteremia to fulminant septic shock, meningitis, multi-organ dysfunction, and severe long-term sequelae. Its rapid clinical course, along with the potential for serious complications-particularly in children-requires high clinical suspicion and immediate intervention. A 5-y-8-month-old boy at DMCH Ludhiana presented with high fever, GI symptoms, irritability, and acute rash. He was in septic shock, showed rapid progression to purpura, DIC, multi-organ injury, and limb gangrene, requiring plastic surgery. N. meningitidis was confirmed by molecular testing, illustrating the disease’s catastrophic potential despite prompt intensive care. In Kolkata, a 2-y-9-month-old girl arrived in shock with fever, rash, and anuria; she developed ARDS and needed prolonged ICU care. N. meningitidis was confirmed in blood culture but CSF examination was normal. Another 8-y-old girl presented with fever, convulsions, and CNS deficits; MRI showed gliosis and CSF PCR was positive for N. meningitidis. These cases highlight severe central nervous system involvement and lasting neurological sequelae. Three more cases with age values around 1 y (4.5 months, 1 y and 1 y 2 months) and coming from different regions of West Bengal were presented with high-grade fever, followed by focal seizure conceived as febrile convulsion initially without any rash. Although blood examination, neuroimaging, CSF analysis appeared normal, only RT-PCR revealed meningococcal infection with no history of vaccination against meningococcus. These cases highlighted the atypical features of IMD cases. Other reported cases from Kolkata included a 4-y-old boy with shock and purpura (CSF examination: normal), infants and young children with seizures and altered sensorium (culture-negative or CSF RT-PCR positive), and an unvaccinated 7-y-old boy with fever, aphasia, and residual neurological deficits. In the Northeast, a 9-month-old boy was admitted with meningitis, shock, bulging fontanel, and florid rash. Gram-d diplococci were seen on stain, prompting public health chemoprophylaxis and outbreak investigation. Across these reported cases, classical symptoms such as septic shock, petechial and purpuric rash, altered sensorium, multi-organ involvement, and rapid deterioration were common. Many children experienced irreversible complications including limb amputation, permanent aphasia, ataxia, and hearing loss, demonstrating the unpredictable and devastating nature of IMD. Atypical presentations (absence of rash, seizure-only presentation, normal initial CSF) of meningitis should not be missed. In the long term, approximately one-third of pediatric survivors develop chronic disabilities, such as neurological deficits, hearing impairment, or limb loss. The lifelong burden of physical disability, psychological distress, and the need for ongoing rehabilitation is substantial for affected families. Scope and objectives of the advisory meeting The expert advisory meeting convened with clear, actionable objectives to address the meningococcal disease challenge in India: Primary objectives Clarify Serogroup Relevance: Determine clinical significance of various meningococcal serogroups (A, B, C, W, X, Y) in Indian epidemiology and vaccination strategy implications. Vaccination Strategy Formulation: Develop evidence-based recommendations on vaccine selection, target populations, immunization schedules, and implementation approaches for Indian settings. full_text_sections.full_text: Meningococcal meningitis in India: An expert consensus on use of MCVs ABSTRACT Invasive meningococcal disease (IMD) is a significant but under-recognized public health challenge in India, marked by rapid progression, high mortality, and severe sequelae. This consensus document, developed from literature review, outbreak analyses, and deliberations by 14 Indian experts, highlights outbreaks from 1966 (Delhi: 616 cases, case fatality ration: CFR 20.9%) to 2022–2023 (Kolkata). Serogroup A remains predominant, with emerging serogroups C, W, and Y. Systematic review evidence shows 12.1% prevalence in epidemics (CFR 12.8%) and 0.76% in endemic settings (CFR 3.0%), though true burden is underestimated due to weak surveillance. IMD shows bimodal age distribution, highest in children < 5 y (61.8%) and adolescents. MenACWY conjugate vaccines show 95.7–99.5% seroprotection across serogroups. Experts recommend vaccination at 9–12 months with booster at 10–11 y, mandatory reporting, sentinel surveillance, and clinician awareness. The roadmap stresses awareness, short-term surveillance, and long-term data generation toward National Immunization Program inclusion. Background and context Neisseria meningitidis, a gram-negative diplococcus, causes life-threatening invasive meningococcal disease (IMD). IMD is characterized by rapid progression, high mortality (4–20%), and devastating long-term complications affecting 10–20% of survivors. Despite being a notifiable disease in India, meningococcal infection remains poorly documented due to diagnostic challenges, limited surveillance infrastructure, and low clinical suspicion outside outbreak settings. This expert consensus emerged from a comprehensive review of pre-published literature, outbreak reports from Indian settings, and deliberations among 14 expert pediatricians, infectious disease specialists, and microbiologists representing diverse geographic regions across India. Epidemiology and disease burden Serogroup A remains the predominant strain associated with outbreaks in India and accounts for most epidemic disease. Sporadic cases involving other serogroups have been increasingly documented. Serogroup C has been reported in pediatric cases from the Institute of Child Health, Kolkata during 2022–2023. Serogroup W-135 has been described in case reports from Tamil Nadu and other regions. Serogroup B has been noted in isolated reports from tertiary centers and, although uncommon, is reported in India. Serogroup X is not clinically significant in India and is relevant mainly to the African meningitis belt. The emergence of non-A serogroups in sporadic cases indicates changing epidemiological patterns and highlights the need for broader vaccine coverage beyond traditional outbreak-associated strains. Evolution of meningococcal serogroups globally. Serogroup Global Evolution Pattern A Dominated African meningitis belt until MenAfriVac introduction (2010); near-elimination by 2015 Also responsible for recurrent large outbreaks in India (Delhi epidemics in 1966–1967, 1985–1986, and 2005–2006 with high case fatality, Meghalaya in 2008–2009, Tripura in 2009). C Caused 20% of global IMD through mid-2010s; reduced by MCC/ACWY vaccine programs. In India, only sporadic serogroup C cases have been reported. (Note: MCC – Meningococcal C conjugate vaccine) W Emerged after 2000 Hajj outbreaks; increased endemic disease in South America, UK, Australia. Serogroup W has been documented infrequently in non‐outbreak settings and case reports, contributing a minor fraction of total reported IMD from India. Y Emerged in 1990s USA; accounts for 20–30% of US IMD cases; driving 2023–2024 US surge. Indian literature notes occasional serogroup Y cases and detectable carriage/antibody responses, but no confirmed serogroup Y outbreak and very low documented clinical burden. B Predominant in Europe, Americas, Australia; accounts for 50–70% of cases in high-income countries. This serotype is considered uncommon in India. X Historically caused sporadic and small outbreaks in the African meningitis belt; major localized epidemics reported in Niger, Burkina Faso, Togo and Kenya since mid‐2000s, with serogroup X responsible for up to ~50–56% of confirmed cases in some district‐level outbreaks. No documented outbreaks or established circulation in India to date. Globally, meningococcal disease showed a significant decline during the COVID-19 pandemic due to non-pharmaceutical interventions such as masking, physical distancing, and reduced travel. A rebound has been observed in the post-pandemic period with several concerning trends. Circulating strains with increased virulence have reemerged. New clonal complexes have appeared following the resumption of international travel. Population immunity has decreased in unvaccinated cohorts. The United States reported the highest number of cases since 2014, with 503 confirmed cases in 2024. There has also been a disproportionate impact on adults aged 30–60 y, Black or African American populations, and individuals with HIV. The summary of evolution of meningococcal serogroups is shown in Table 1. Historically, the evolution of meningococcal serogroups has shown dynamic global shifts. Serogroup A dominated the African meningitis belt until the introduction of MenAfriVac (Serogroup A conjugate vaccine) in 2010, leading to near-elimination by 2015. Serogroup C contributed to about 20% of global IMD through the mid-2010s but declined following MCC and ACWY vaccination programs. Serogroup W emerged after the 2000 Hajj outbreaks and later increased in endemic regions such as South America, the United Kingdom, and Australia. Serogroup Y, which emerged in the United States in the 1990s, now accounts for 20–30% of U.S. cases and is a major driver of the 2023–2024 surge. Serogroup B remains predominant in Europe, the Americas, and Australia and contributes to 50%–70% of cases in high-income countries. In the Asia-Pacific region, meningococcal disease remains under-recognized, largely due to inadequate surveillance systems. Serogroup A has historically been predominant in China, India, Nepal, Mongolia, and Pakistan. Emerging serogroups, including C, Y, and W, have been reported in several countries. Serogroup B is uncommon in most of Asia except in developed nations such as Australia, New Zealand, and Japan. The overall disease burden in the region is likely significantly underestimated. papers.title: Real-world influenza surveillance and vaccine effectiveness in children: a multicentre study of the Italian Federation of Primary Care Paediatricians (FIMP).
papers.abstract: Objectives Influenza is a significant cause of morbidity among children and a significant factor in primary care consultations. While numerous studies on influenza vaccine effectiveness have been conducted, the majority of the available data comes from hospital settings; the objective of this study is to estimate influenza vaccine effectiveness in children in paediatric primary care settings. Methods A multicentre observational study was conducted among family paediatricians working in outpatient clinics in various Italian regions during the 2024/25 influenza season. Children aged 2-7 years with influenza-like illness were enrolled and underwent rapid antigen point-of-care tests (POCT). Children who were positive on POCT underwent molecular RT-PCR tests for influenza in a centralized laboratory. Vaccine effectiveness (VE) was estimated as 1-odds ratio by a test-negative case-control design and as 1-incidence rate ratio by a cohort study, in which the aggregated denominator of the children included in the beneficiary lists of the participant pediatriacians was used to compute the incidence in vaccinated and non-vaccinated. Results The circulation of influenza was characterized by a clear seasonal pattern, with sustained activity of the virus throughout the period. 739 ILI cases were tested. The results showed a 79% (95%CI: 70-86) reduction of laboratory-confirmed influenza ILI, i.e vaccine efficacy (1-OR). The results were consistent when sensitivity analysis was performed for different types of influenza vaccine and when results obtained by POCT were compared to results obtained by RT-PCR confirmation. When the results were assessed by the cohort method, vaccination was associated with a marked reduction in incidence of influenza with VE 76% (1-IRR); 95%CI 67-82) and no reduction of ILI that tested negative for influenza virus. Conclusions This study shows high VE of the 24-25 influenza vaccines against symptomatic disease in healthy children, demonstrating the feasibility to perform influenza surveillance in a paediatric primary care setting in real-life conditions.

papers.abstract_zh: 目标 流感是儿童发病的一个重要原因,也是初级保健咨询的一个重要因素。虽然已经进行了大量关于流感疫苗有效性的研究,但大多数可用数据来自医院环境;本研究的目的是评估儿科初级保健机构中儿童流感疫苗的有效性。方法 对 2024/25 流感季节期间在意大利各地区门诊诊所工作的家庭儿科医生进行了一项多中心观察性研究。患有流感样疾病的 2-7 岁儿童被纳入研究并接受快速抗原即时检测 (POCT)。POCT 呈阳性的儿童在中心实验室接受了流感分子 RT-PCR 检测。疫苗有效性(VE)通过测试阴性病例对照设计估计为 1 比值比,通过队列研究估计为 1 发病率比,其中使用参与儿科医生受益名单中儿童的总分母来计算接种疫苗和未接种疫苗的发病率。结果流感流行具有明显的季节性特征,病毒在整个时期内持续活动。739 例流感样病例接受了检测。结果显示,实验室确诊的流感 ILI,即疫苗功效 (1-OR) 降低了 79% (95% CI: 70-86)。当对不同类型的流感疫苗进行敏感性分析以及将POCT获得的结果与RT-PCR确认获得的结果进行比较时,结果是一致的。当通过队列方法评估结果时,疫苗接种与流感发病率显着降低相关,VE 为 76% (1-IRR);95%CI 67-82),流感病毒检测呈阴性的 ILI 没有减少。结论 本研究显示 24-25 流感疫苗对健康儿童的症状性疾病具有较高的 VE,证明了在现实生活条件下在儿科初级保健环境中进行流感监测的可行性。

papers.title: Prevalence, incidence, mortality, and years of life lost to diabetes from 1996 to 2024 in Denmark.
papers.abstract: Introduction Population-based surveillance is essential for quantifying the burden of diabetes and monitoring temporal changes. In Denmark, nationwide health registers enable long-term surveillance of type 1 diabetes (T1D) and type 2 diabetes (T2D). We aimed to estimate trends in prevalence, incidence, mortality and years of life lost to diabetes in Denmark from 1996 to 2024. Research design and methods We conducted a nationwide register-based cohort study from 1996 to 2024. We used an updated national diabetes register integrating hospital, prescription, clinical, and laboratory data to identify diabetes type and date of onset. Prevalence was estimated annually using a binomial model. Incidence, mortality and standardized mortality ratios (SMR) were analyzed using age-period-cohort models. Analyses were stratified by sex and diabetes type. A multistate model was used to assess the lifetime risk and years of life lost to diabetes. Results As of January 1, 2025, a total of 366 174 individuals (6.1% of the population) had diabetes identified through national healthcare registers; of these, 8.2% had T1D and 91.8% had T2D. Since 1996, diabetes prevalence more than tripled, largely driven by an overall annual increase in T2D of ~4.1%. T1D prevalence remained stable, with increases in individuals aged Conclusions In Denmark, diabetes prevalence and incidence increased markedly since 1996, largely driven by T2D. Although mortality declined, particularly for T1D, excess mortality remains, emphasizing the need for continued surveillance and prevention efforts.
